claims: Direction changes the movement and stability contract and must be declared rather than inferred from a generic line-hop name.
Exact survivor cards require two-foot takeoff and landing, a visible line, one declared crossing direction, repeated low-amplitude contacts, contact accounting, and a controlled finish.
Repeated hopping belongs to stretch-shortening-cycle plyometric work, but a family label does not establish direction, foot count, line crossing, cadence, or terminal action.
The controlled identities separate lateral side-to-side and sagittal forward-back travel; generic sources missing those fields remain nonselectable.
Two-foot hopping uses lower-limb spring behavior with substantial plantar-flexor activity and task-dependent contributions from the foot, ankle, knee, hip, and trunk.

Exact cards declare bilateral lower-limb contacts, sagittal ankle-knee actions, direction-specific frontal or sagittal stabilization, and whole-body postural control without claiming isolated activation.
Shorter hopping contact conditions were associated with greater leg stiffness and higher gastrocnemius and soleus activity in the studied task.
Contact-time intent, amplitude, landing alignment, line clearance, direction, and surface are observable execution variables; exact thresholds are not inferred for these cards.
Direction affects postural-stability demand and therefore contributes to exercise complexity.
Score exercise complexity and physical difficulty only, derive overall as their maximum, and never store athlete skill or proficiency on exercise cards.
Plyometric exposure is meaningfully described by ground-contact volume and intervention time, but broad meta-analytic totals are not a per-session prescription for one athlete.
Track bilateral landing contacts, direction, surface, amplitude, contact quality, set duration, symptoms, output loss, prior impact, and recovery response.
Plyometric work requires appropriate progression, surface, space, preparation, and movement control.
Require a visible floor line, level high-traction resilient surface, clear landing area on both sides, safe footwear, no traffic, and enough coach visibility for the group.
Ground contacts are the primary exposure unit for repeated hopping and cumulative volume must be controlled.
Use small quality sets with declared contacts, full enough rest to preserve contact rhythm and alignment, and a conservative session contact ceiling that includes other jumps and landings.
Executable hopping instruction declares start, posture, direction, line crossing, bilateral contact, amplitude, rhythm, contact accounting, finish, and reset.
Cue tall posture, quiet low-amplitude contacts, feet landing together, line clearance, direction-specific control, and an immediate stop when quality changes.
Plyometric exercise should be progressed to readiness and performed with suitable surface, technique, volume, and recovery.

Stop for pain, instability, numbness, dizziness, Achilles or plantar symptoms, repeated line contact, asymmetric landing, foot separation, excessive knee or hip collapse, rising contact time, lost rhythm, unsafe surface, or traffic.
Plyometric jump training can improve reactive-strength outcomes, but exercise selection and dose must match context and accumulated exposure.
Place crisp line pogos while fresh, before heavy lower-body fatigue or dense conditioning, and count every landing toward session and weekly impact budgets.
Athletes need visible setup, a simple contact-count rule, expected effort and sensations, and clear stop guidance.
Render direction, foot count, line crossing, contacts per set, sets, rest, amplitude, surface, finish, and symptom escalation before starting.
Contact and flight timing can characterize hopping behavior, but measurement method and task must be declared.
Observe line clearance, simultaneous feet, contact count, amplitude, rhythm, posture, direction drift, alignment, symptoms, output drop, finish, and cumulative impact exposure.
Plyometric tasks should be individualized and progressed from controlled lower-demand options.

Options include fewer contacts, lower amplitude, slower declared rhythm, longer rest, a wider visual target, an in-place bilateral pogo, calf-raise rhythm work, text or still-image instruction, and coach demonstration after review.
Lateral and forward-back directions are not interchangeable delivery labels because direction changes the task.

Single-leg, alternating, in-place, diagonal, rotational, continuous-travel, hurdle, weighted, reactive-cue, and terminal-stick versions require exact variants or separate definitions; line width, contact count, set duration, amplitude, rest, and starting side are modifiers after identity is fixed.
YouTube supports privacy-enhanced embedding through youtube-nocookie.com.

Retained links returned current oEmbed metadata on 2026-08-01, but availability and title do not establish exact foot count, direction, crossing, amplitude, safety, accessibility, quality, reviewer, or approval.
